hook: A movie ticket that cost $\$5$ when your parents were teenagers costs about $\$15$ today. Did movies get three times better, or did money buy less? To answer, economists price the same basket of goods year after year. That one idea, a fixed basket, gives the consumer price index, the inflation rate, and a way to tell whether a raise actually makes you better off.

options: Household spending on goods and services
prereq.why: Consumption (C) is what households spend. The CPI tracks the prices of a basket of what households buy.

prereq.q: Why does a smartphone that costs the same as ten years ago show a limitation of GDP?
options: GDP counts the price paid and can miss gains in quality
GDP leaves out goods made abroad
prereq.why: Market values can miss quality gains. The same problem shows up in price indexes.

figure.caption: The same basket priced in three years: dividing each cost by the base-year cost and multiplying by 100 gives the CPI.

chain.cause: A fixed basket of goods is priced each year
chain.effect: its cost this year divided by its cost in the base year, times 100, is the consumer price index

chain.cause: The index rises from one year to the next
chain.effect: the percent change in the index is the inflation rate

chain.cause: Prices rise faster than a person's pay
chain.effect: their real wage (nominal wage divided by the index, times 100) falls

chain.cause: Consumers switch away from goods whose prices rose
chain.effect: the fixed basket overstates the rise in the cost of living (substitution bias)

ideas: CPI $= \frac{\text{cost of basket this year}}{\text{cost in base year}} \times 100$. The base year is 100.
Inflation rate $= \frac{\text{new index} - \text{old index}}{\text{old index}} \times 100$. Divide by the old index, not 100.
Real value $= \frac{\text{nominal value}}{\text{price index}} \times 100$: what money buys in base-year dollars.
Deflation: prices fall. Disinflation: inflation slows but prices still rise. Substitution bias and quality gains make the CPI overstate inflation.

misconception.wrong: A CPI of 130 means prices rose 130%, and a falling inflation rate means prices are falling.
misconception.right: A CPI of 130 means prices are 30% above the base year. A falling inflation rate is disinflation: prices still rise, just more slowly. Only deflation means prices fall.

summary: A price index compares the cost of a fixed basket with its cost in the base year (index 100). The consumer price index uses a basket households buy; the inflation rate is the percent change in the index. Dividing a nominal value by the index and multiplying by 100 gives a real value. Substitution bias, new goods and quality gains make the CPI overstate inflation.
